Plug-in solar planner

Plug-in solar has been legal in Great Britain since 27 August 2026. Enter where and how you want to put the panels, and the planner checks your set-up against the planning rules in England and the rules for kits.

What the planner checks

Being allowed to plug a kit into a socket does not automatically mean the place you fix it is allowed. That is decided by planning rules, which in England were changed on the same day. The planner works out the measurements that matter from your panel size and tilt:

  • Garden: no more than 9 m² of panels in total. The highest point may be 1 m within 5 m of the boundary in front of the house, 2 m within 5 m of the boundary elsewhere, and 4 m anywhere else in the garden.
  • Wall or balcony: panels may stick out no more than 0.4 m from the wall, or 0.2 m on a wall facing a road.
  • Flat roof: no more than 0.6 m above the highest part of the roof.
  • No wood: plug-in panels fixed to a wooden fence, gate, wall, balcony or timber cladding are not permitted development.

Why panels on a wall are trickier than they look

A typical panel is about 1.7 to 1.8 m long. Tilted out from a wall at a good angle for sunshine, it sticks out far more than 0.4 m. At 30° from horizontal, a 1.72 m panel reaches out almost 1.5 m. To stay within 0.4 m, bracket included, it has to hang at about 78° or steeper, which is close to vertical. Turned to landscape, the 1.13 m side runs down the slope, and about 72° is enough. The planner shows you the minimum angle for your panel.

Near-vertical panels produce less than panels tilted at about 30 to 35°. That is why the Energy Saving Trust sees gardens as the most suitable place for today's kits.

What about a timber frame in the garden?

We build timber calculators, so this was our first idea too. The new rules exclude plug-in panels fixed to a wooden fence, gate, wall or other enclosure, and the kit rules exclude timber cladding and timber balconies, for fire safety. Whether a free-standing timber frame counts is not spelled out. Until that is clear, we recommend the metal mounting system from your kit's manufacturer. If you want to use your own frame, ask your council for a certificate of lawfulness first.

More background on choosing a kit, mounting it safely and what it saves is in our plug-in solar guide.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need planning permission for plug-in solar?
In England, usually not, as long as the panels stay within the permitted development limits for size, height and projection, are not fixed to timber, and the property is not listed. In protected areas, panels within 5 m of the boundary need prior approval. Wales and Scotland have their own rules.
How big can a plug-in solar kit be?
The inverter may feed in no more than 800 VA. The panels may add up to 2,000 W across up to four panels, with no more than two in series. Only one kit is allowed per home.
Can I fix plug-in solar to my garden fence?
Not to a wooden fence. In England that is excluded from permitted development because of the fire risk. A masonry wall or a stand on the ground is the better choice.
Is the planner legal advice?
No. It checks the main measurements against the published rules. Local restrictions such as Article 4 directions can remove permitted development rights. If in doubt, ask your council for a certificate of lawfulness.

All timber sections are guide values and do not replace a structural calculation. Carports and patio covers may need planning permission and building regulations approval, and a structural engineer's check depending on where you live.
